title: Two Sum
problem: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.
approach: Use a hash map to store previously seen numbers and their indices. For each number, check whether target - number already exists.
interview_tip: Hashing can reduce the brute-force O(n²) solution to O(n).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problem: Given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on the ith day, find the maximum profit that can be achieved by buying on one day and selling on a later day.
approach: Maintain the minimum price seen so far and calculate the maximum profit at every day.
interview_tip: Track the minimum value seen so far instead of checking every pair.

title: Contains Duplicate
problem: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice and false if every element is distinct.
approach: Use an unordered_set. While traversing the array, if an element already exists in the set, a duplicate is present.
interview_tip: A hash set provides average O(1) lookup.

title: Maximum Subarray
problem: Given an integer array nums, find the subarray with the largest sum and return its sum.
approach: Use Kadane's algorithm. Maintain the best sum ending at the current position and update the global maximum.
interview_tip: Kadane's algorithm is a must-know array pattern.

title: Product of Array Except Self
problem: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all elements of nums except nums[i].
approach: Build prefix products from the left and multiply them with suffix products from the right without using division.
interview_tip: Prefix and suffix techniques are useful when an answer depends on all elements except the current one.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
problem: Given an integer array nums, find a contiguous non-empty subarray that has the largest product and return the product.
approach: Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at each position because a negative number can turn the minimum into the maximum.
interview_tip: When multiplication and negative values are involved, track both maximum and minimum states.

title: Move Zeroes
problem: Given an integer array nums, move all zeroes to the end while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements.
approach: Use a pointer to place non-zero elements at the front, then fill the remaining positions with zeroes.
interview_tip: The slow-fast pointer pattern is common in array problems.

title: Majority Element
problem: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element. The majority element appears more than n/2 times.
approach: Use Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm. Maintain a candidate and count, cancelling different elements against the candidate.
interview_tip: Boyer-Moore is an important O(1) space voting technique.

title: 3Sum
problem: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that their sum is zero.
approach: Sort the array and fix one element. Use two pointers for the remaining two elements while skipping duplicates.
interview_tip: Sorting plus two pointers is a core pattern for pair and triplet problems.

title: Container With Most Water
problem: Given an integer array height, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container containing the most water.
approach: Start with pointers at both ends. Calculate the area and move the pointer with the smaller height.
interview_tip: When maximizing distance-based pair values, consider whether two pointers can eliminate impossible candidates.

title: Valid Palindrome
problem: Given a string s, determine if it is a palindrome considering only alphanumeric characters and ignoring cases.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

approach: Use two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing lowercase characters.
interview_tip: Two pointers are often the simplest solution for palindrome problems.

title: Valid Anagram
problem: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s and false otherwise.
approach: Count the frequency of each character in both strings and compare the counts.
interview_tip: Frequency counting is one of the most common string problem patterns.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problem: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
approach: Use a sliding window with a frequency array or hash map. Expand the right pointer and move the left pointer when a duplicate appears.
interview_tip: Sliding window is essential for substring and subarray problems with constraints.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problem: Given a string s and an integer k, you can replace at most k characters. Return the length of the longest substring containing the same letter after replacements.
approach: Maintain a sliding window and the frequency of its most common character. If window size minus maximum frequency exceeds k, shrink the window.
interview_tip: A useful sliding-window condition is window_size - most_frequent_count <= k.

title: Binary Search
problem: Given a sorted array of integers nums and an integer target, return the index of target if it exists, otherwise return -1.
approach: Maintain a search range using left and right pointers. Compare the middle element with the target and eliminate half of the search space.
interview_tip: Know both the standard binary search template and how to avoid integer overflow in mid calculation.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problem: Given an array nums sorted in ascending order and rotated at an unknown pivot, search for target and return its index.
approach: At every step one half of the array is guaranteed to be sorted. Determine which half is sorted and check whether the target belongs to that range.
interview_tip: In rotated binary search, first identify which half is sorted.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problem: Given a sorted array that has been rotated between 1 and n times, find the minimum element.
approach: Compare the middle element with the rightmost element to determine which half contains the minimum.
interview_tip: Binary search can locate a boundary or extremum, not just an exact target.

title: Reverse Linked List
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the reversed list.
approach: Use three pointers: previous, current, and next. Reverse each current node's pointer and move forward.
interview_tip: Always save curr->next before changing the pointer.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problem: Merge two sorted linked lists and return the head of the merged sorted list.
approach: Use a dummy node and repeatedly attach the smaller current node from the two lists.
interview_tip: Dummy nodes simplify linked-list insertion and merging.

title: Linked List Cycle
problem: Given the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list contains a cycle.

examples.input: head = [3,2,0,-4], tail connects to node index 1

approach: Use Floyd's slow and fast pointer algorithm. If the pointers meet, a cycle exists.
interview_tip: Floyd's cycle detection algorithm is a fundamental linked-list technique.

title: Middle of the Linked List
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node.
approach: Use slow and fast pointers. Slow moves one step while fast moves two steps. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.
interview_tip: Slow-fast pointers can solve many linked-list problems in one pass.

title: Valid Parentheses
problem: Given a string containing parentheses, determine if the input string is valid. Every opening bracket must be closed by the same type of bracket in the correct order.
approach: Use a stack. Push opening brackets and ensure every closing bracket matches the top of the stack.
interview_tip: Stacks are ideal when the latest unmatched opening element must be processed first.

title: Min Stack
problem: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time.
approach: Maintain a second stack containing the minimum value at each stack level.
interview_tip: An auxiliary data structure can maintain additional state while preserving O(1) operations.

title: Daily Temperatures
problem: Given an array of daily temperatures, return an array where answer[i] tells how many days you have to wait after day i to get a warmer temperature.
approach: Use a decreasing monotonic stack of indices. When the current temperature is greater than the temperature at the stack top, resolve that previous day.
interview_tip: Monotonic stacks are useful for next greater/smaller element problems.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values.
approach: Use a queue for BFS. Process all nodes currently in the queue as one level before moving to the next level.
interview_tip: BFS with a queue is the standard approach for level-order traversal.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth.
approach: Use recursion. The depth of a node is one plus the maximum depth of its left and right subtrees.
interview_tip: Many tree problems can be expressed naturally using recursive subtree relationships.

title: Invert Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree and return its root.
approach: Recursively invert the left and right subtrees and then swap the two child pointers.
interview_tip: Think of tree recursion as solving the same problem independently for each subtree.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
problem: Given a binary search tree and two nodes p and q, find their lowest common ancestor.
approach: Use the BST ordering property. If both nodes are smaller, move left. If both are larger, move right. Otherwise the current node is the LCA.
interview_tip: Always look for properties of BSTs that can eliminate unnecessary traversal.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid binary search tree.
approach: Recursively maintain a valid range for each node. Every node must be strictly greater than its lower bound and smaller than its upper bound.
interview_tip: For BST validation, checking only immediate children is insufficient; maintain the full valid range.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problem: Given the root of a binary search tree, return the kth smallest value among all the node values.
approach: An inorder traversal of a BST visits nodes in sorted order. Stop when the kth node is visited.
interview_tip: Remember: inorder traversal of a BST produces values in sorted ascending order.
